name: App Standby Buckets
plain: Android sorts apps into five buckets that cap job time, alarms and network by how recently they were used.
meaning: Rarely opened apps get tiny background budgets, so a retention team sees its sync silently slow down for dormant users. Active apps in the top bucket have almost none.

android.prompt_ui: None; set by the system from usage
android.revocation: Settings > Apps; adb shell am get-standby-bucket
android.note: Job runtime: Working 10 min per 4 h; Frequent 10 min per 12 h; Rare 10 min per 24 h; Restricted once per day. Alarms: Working 10 per hour, Frequent 2, Rare 1, Restricted 1 per day. Network off for Rare and Restricted

ios.note: iOS has no per-app bucket; see Background App Refresh and Low Power Mode

fields.name: bucket
fields.range: Active, Working set, Frequent, Rare, Restricted, Never

limits.headline: Can't run as much in the background if you rarely open the app
limits.user_action: Nothing. Android sorts apps into groups by how recently you opened them
can: Run about 10 minutes per 4 hours if you use it often
Run jobs and alarms more freely when it sits in the Working group
Move back to a better group after you use the app again
cannot: Pick its own group; Android sets that from your use
Run more than about 10 minutes per 24 hours when the app is rarely used
Run only once a day when it is in the Restricted group
Face this on iPhone, which has no groups like this
limits.differs: Android has five usage groups that cap jobs, alarms and network. iPhone has no per app group.

story.what_it_is: Android sorts apps into groups by how often you use them and limits background work for the rarely used ones.

marketing.name: App Standby Buckets
marketing.pitch: Google describes buckets as a way to prioritize resources for apps people use most and limit those they do not.

story.for_you: You never see the groups. But an app you have not opened in weeks will be slower to sync and alert you, while apps you use daily keep working normally.
story.for_makers: Makers see their reach shrink for dormant users, since background jobs, alarms and network all get cut. They lean on push messages and design the app to catch up the moment it opens.

use_cases.example: A news app has fresh stories ready for daily readers but needs a moment to catch up for people who rarely open it.
A store sends fewer background price refreshes to users in the rare bucket.
A game you stopped playing weeks ago stops its timed energy refills in the background.
A chat app must use high priority push to reach someone in a quiet bucket.
A retention team notices background sync slows for dormant users and adjusts its win back campaign.
An ad SDK can upload events less often for apps in low buckets.

risks: Late alerts for rarely used apps
Dormant users are harder to reach
story.android_note: Android only. Five buckets with strict job, alarm and network limits.
story.ios_note: iOS has no buckets. It relies on Background App Refresh and Low Power Mode.

technical_bounds: Active has quota only from Android 16

history.change: Restricted bucket assigned automatically after 45 days idle
Job quotas enforced for Active bucket (20 min per 60 min) and based on top state and FGS
